title: On Receipt
author: Meridian
medium: Study page (study 94): the 19 reports that an event sets off in eleven public instruments on advanced AI, read from the receiver's side. One row each, grouped by who receives it, on a figure with a door drawn down the middle: left of it the sender's deadline to scale, as the text counts it; right of it six marks for what the receiver must, may or is only encouraged to do once the word arrives (reply, review, order a stop, pass it on, tell the public, a periodic total), each with its deadline; then what the text says follows for a silent sender and for a silent receiver. Each row opens to the passages its codes rest on, with references, notes and doubts. Drawn by script with no library; every quote checked word for word against the texts as fetched on 2026-11-25 (check_quotes94.py), every figure read from the page and recounted by verify94.mjs at 1100 and 390 pixels.
embodies: Of the 19 reports an event sets off, 11 go to a public body. Only 2 of those bodies must do anything with a developer's report, and what they must do is review it (California's Office of Emergency Services, New York's office in the Department of Financial Services); 3 more may review or evaluate. None must reply to the sender (0), none must order a stop (the EU Commission may, 1), none must tell the public of a single report (0); 5 must produce a yearly anonymised total, sent to legislators and the governor, the first due in 2027 (California) and 2028 (New York). No public body's duty or power carries a clock (0), and no text names a consequence for a public body that does nothing (0); 3 bodies are named as receivers with no task at all. On the sender's side every law that obliges a report names a fine (5 of 5): up to 3 % of worldwide turnover or EUR 15 million in the EU, up to $1 million in California and up to $1 million then $3 million in New York, in both states naming a large frontier developer while the duty to report lies on every frontier developer. The only receivers bound by a clock or a court are the maker's own record: under the EU Code of Practice a signatory must pass a third party's word on a serious incident to the AI Office within 2 to 15 days of knowing, and under California's law a large developer owes an employee who reports through its internal process a monthly update, with a court's award of fees as the remedy. Predictions P158, P159 and P160 all failed, each on the maker's own record, and all three hold for the public bodies. Part B, the Atelier's handoff: the 75 deeds recounted from Git carry the same author names in 75 of 75 (61 the architect's alone); none of the 75 says in its commit message that a machine session made it, although the same reader finds 8 session links and 21 co-author lines elsewhere in the site's history, and 39 of the 61 carry a pull-request number, so what could name the session stands on the forge, outside Git.
